task_row_model.query: In a multi-center randomized clinical trial with longitudinal follow-up and a treatment-by-time interaction, how should I specify a linear mixed-effects model to estimate treatment effect trajectories? Specifically, what fixed and random effects and covariance structure are recommended, and which small-sample denominator degrees-of-freedom methods (Kenward–Roger vs Satterthwaite) are appropriate for inference on fixed effects?

documents.content: When centers are few and were part of the randomization stratification, it is often preferable to include center as a fixed effect rather than a random effect because variance-component estimates are unstable with a small number of clusters. For longitudinal measurements at the subject level, include fixed effects for baseline covariates, time (as categorical if non-linear trajectory is expected), treatment, and treatment-by-time interaction. Specify subject-level random intercepts and, if individual slopes vary, random slopes for time with an unstructured covariance for those random effects. Use REML for parameter estimation of the covariance structure but be cautious when comparing models that differ in fixed effects, where ML may be required.

A recommended LME specification for estimating treatment-by-time trajectories is: fixed effects for treatment, time (categorical or polynomial continuous), treatment*time, important baseline covariates, and center as fixed if there are few centers or as a random effect if many. Random effects typically include subject-level random intercepts and, if warranted, random slopes for time; allow covariance between intercept and slope. For within-subject residuals choose an unstructured covariance if there are few timepoints, otherwise consider AR(1) or heterogeneous compound symmetry. For inference in small samples use Kenward–Roger adjustment with REML because it corrects both the covariance estimator and denominator degrees of freedom; Satterthwaite is an alternative that adjusts DF but not the covariance estimator. Software: SAS PROC MIXED supports DDFM=KENWARDROGER; in R use lmerTest or pbkrtest for approximations.

Generalized estimating equations (GEE) provide population-averaged estimates for longitudinal data and are robust to misspecification of the working correlation, but they do not model subject-specific trajectories and cannot easily accommodate complex random-effects structures like varying intercepts and slopes. GEE standard errors are typically obtained via robust sandwich estimators, which perform well asymptotically but may be biased in small samples or with few clusters. If the scientific question concerns subject-specific treatment trajectories or prediction, mixed-effects models are preferable; if only marginal effects are of interest and sample size is large, GEE is an alternative.

For a multi-center longitudinal randomized trial, specify fixed effects for treatment, time (prefer categorical for flexible trajectories), treatment-by-time interaction to capture differential trajectories, baseline covariates and, depending on the number of centers, center as fixed (few centers) or center random effect (many centers). Include subject-level random intercepts and, when slope variability exists, random slopes for time with covariance between intercept and slope. Choose within-subject residual structure: unstructured for few timepoints, AR(1) or heterogeneous CS otherwise. Use REML for estimating variance components; for hypothesis tests on fixed effects in moderate-to-small samples, Kenward–Roger is generally preferred because it adjusts both the estimated covariance matrix and denominator degrees of freedom, improving Type I error control. Satterthwaite is a common alternative that provides DF approximation but does not make the same covariance matrix correction.

Survival analysis with center-level frailty terms is an appropriate framework when the primary endpoint is time-to-event and there is center heterogeneity. A shared frailty Cox model introduces a multiplicative random effect at the center level to account for between-center variability; baseline hazards remain unspecified. For repeated events or longitudinal biomarkers predictive of survival, joint models that combine a mixed-effects submodel for the biomarker and a survival submodel allow estimation of the association between the longitudinal trajectory and hazard. These approaches are distinct from linear mixed models for continuous longitudinal outcomes and require careful consideration of censoring and proportional hazards assumptions.
